### 2026-10-09 – Today was my first day working on Half Life as I've been really busy recently, but I was very excited to get started!

**1.6h**

Today was my first day working on Half Life as I've been really busy recently, but I was very excited to get started!

I read through the Half Life instructions, installed KiCad (as well as all the folders in the week 1 care package) and got to work. I have never worked with pcbs before, but the tutorial was really easy to follow. I managed to get everything done in the schematic editor although I had a little trouble finding one of the parts called "R" that wasn't listed in the tutorial, but that's okay! Here's the finished product:

![Screenshot 2026-10-09 140539](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/dFzFUhCcKmaw8Zuhg60Jet6VnSvHw5jp/03c3ce1d0d165742993d5bff0a2f425765ed130cdd617f1b422dbce78cffadee.png)

 Then I started with the pcb editor, and that's when things started to get tricky. Everything needs to be routed together for it to work, but it's a lot of connections that can't cross each other and it turned messy pretty fast. Finally, when I thought I'd cabled everything together like the reference photo, I realized that I'd only actually done a portion of it. I'd left maybe half of the connectors just sitting there, because what I didn't realize was that the photo seemed to have connected everything in multiple layers to allow all the cables to cross over each other. Here's what I had by the end of the session (as you can see, the routing is very much not done):

![Screenshot 2026-10-09 140454](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/dFzFUhCcKmaw8Zuhg60Jet6VnSvHw5jp/6ee908b24bcbe3ba3530a5d295288f4c6ccd55ab074a386db32ca5a2c2333d7a.png)

 The github mentioned something about a GND pour, but I tried that using the provided video tutorial and it didn't seem to work. It also took a really long time to outline since I was making a circle shape, so I switched to a square for easier use. My goal for next time is to figure out how to make the layers and to finish routing my pcb, with a bonus for figuring out how to do it as a circle since my goal is to make a circular pcb that I can encase in a 3D printed shell to make a little planet keychain!

### 2026-10-10 – I really wanted to finish the design part of this project before the end of the day, and I'm so glad I did!

**1.25h**

I really wanted to finish the design part of this project before the end of the day, and I'm so glad I did!

Or at least part of it—I got through the routing, which was the hard part for sure. I was totally stuck on the connections that seemed to be on different layers, until I realized the pcb actually has two main layers, and I just needed to edit the other layer to add that missing connection.  That still didn't fix all my errors though, but I was able to join a Slack call on the #half-life channel for about an hour and that was super helpfu! A very kind community member helped teach me some of the basics of pcbs, so here's a bit of what I learned:

- A pcb has two sides, a front, and a back. These are the two layers I was seeing in my editor, and you can solder or connect things on both sides.
- There are two main kinds of pcb parts, through parts and parts that are only on one side of the pcb. Through parts are basically holes in the pcb, so they can connect electrical signals from one side to the other.
- While it's gotten easier to do in the modern day, you should avoid 90 degree routing.
- A ground pour (which I had previously made without understanding what it was) is kind of like a layer of copper. You only want to do it on one side of the pcb, because it's all you need and otherwise you'd be wasting copper. It can connect all the GND ports so you don't actually have to wire them (this is only for the ones that are through parts though).
- The USB input on the main Xiao piece needs to be outside the edge cut, because that's where you're going to plug in your device. If you leave it inside your pcb, you won't be able to access it or charge your device.

This may seem like really basic stuff to anyone who knows what they're doing, but when I tell you I had never touched a piece of hardware ever before this, I mean it. I'm starting from zero over here, but hey, we all have to start somewhere right?

While I wasn't able to get everything solved, the whole info session was incredible because, up until this point, I had no idea what I was doing since the tutorial didn't describe how any of the stuff I was designing actually worked (if anyone who worked on the Starbie tutorial is reading this, that would be a helpful thing to add for beginners). That combined with a little googling, I realized that the GND ports actually automatically link to a GND pour as long as the tag or name is the same, so I was able to FINALLY finish the routing without any more issues. Here's a photo:

![Screenshot 2026-10-09 223942](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/dFzFUhCcKmaw8Zuhg60Jet6VnSvHw5jp/40a9f87513b9c060592aa25b5b8fcf03fe3bbbb8be4d4f2021ec0992d7194bf3.png)

I'm so glad it's finally done! It stayed a rectangle because the circle really was just too painful for GND pours and I had to redo the pours constantly (a lot of trial and error on this one). Also, with a circle I would be worried about accessing the USB port, but maybe this is something that can still be done and the port just has to stick out a little as opposed to all the way? I'll look into it later, maybe after finishing the rest of the project. I was also able to view my PCB in 3D for the first time, and would you look at that!

![Screenshot 2026-10-09 223958](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/dFzFUhCcKmaw8Zuhg60Jet6VnSvHw5jp/9cf0e63a76075b58fa84a516c3f9162a99285c9a5a6972443fa5df3d5a8da05b.png)

Combining this with what I learned, I understand which parts are through holes, which parts are on the front, which parts are on the back... I feel like I'm learning a lot which is absolutely what I came here for. I think it would have taken me a long time to finally get to learning this stuff on my own so Half Life has been a great opportunity.

Can't wait to keep going (tomorrow though because I am very tired right now and I need sleep)!

### 2026-10-10 – Today I finished all the software for the pcb!

**1.23h**

Today I finished all the software for the pcb!

I'm super proud to say that it's all done! I started the session by continuing through the tutorial, which mentioned you could add images to your pcb. I thought that was super cute but didn't realize that the photos needed to be black and white, so I lost a little time on that. Not to worry though, five minutes later I picked out a couple kirby themed stickers and this little planet to add to the front of the pcb. I think it gives my Starbie character (although I mostly did it for the sake of learning how to do it because any extra understanding I can get on how this all works is a positive).

Here's a photo with the stickers:
![Screenshot 2026-10-10 182508](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/dFzFUhCcKmaw8Zuhg60Jet6VnSvHw5jp/0a245441fbf794f718626f5b6c9c8fdac5d4a71264e58ecb3b8881ba84faf730.png)

After that, it was on to the software section! I was very grateful to discover that most of the code had already been written out because it ended up being somewhere between 400-600 lines of code and there's no way I would have been able to figure it all out by myself, even if I'd had the full week. I downloaded the Arduino IDE for the first time, watched some basic videos while all the packages loaded (which took longer than I thought it would) and then pasted in the code. Following the comments, I didn't really end up changing too much. I did have to edit some of the port numbers as I switched which ports went where on my pcb for easier wiring, but I tried to avoid doing this too much on the main Xiao piece so thankfully it wasn't too bad. I didn't want to just use the code there and call it a day, but I couldn't really understand much of it (mostly lack of syntax knowledge I think although I was relieved to see the syntax was very similar to Processing, a language I've explored more with), so instead I decided to make my own sprite for the pcb! For some reason I decided I needed this thing to have a peacock on it, but I found a reference video online and it wasn't too hard to draw. In fact, I think he (or she) turned out pretty cute.

![Screenshot 2026-10-10 202639](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/dFzFUhCcKmaw8Zuhg60Jet6VnSvHw5jp/08d04e181bb5cb9a6678173cb38b80f45b76853ce242356722fae71473e0c8b0.png)

I still need to find a name for the sprite, but that can be a later problem (along with debugging, which I'm sure I'll need to do a lot of). I ended the session by exporting all the extra necessary files from KiCad. I found a video tutorial that showed me how to export the gerber, composition, and BOM files, so I did that and actually found a website where I could test the gerber files to make sure they were accurate (thankfully they were). Then I uploaded it all to my github repository, and that's that! I'm going to look through the docs and see if there's anything else I need to do like a README (mine is maybe a sentence and I have a feeling that's far too short) or if I need to organize things a specific way. I also saw that the repo actually already had a BOM thing that said it synced with half life, so if I could find out how to edit that as well that would be great because I couldn't find a website that could accurately tell me how much the pcb would cost, especially just for one. Best get to work then!
